Fees, the city, the shortest study time and the answer key are checked by public.enroll_quick_course() / complete_quick_course() from public.quick_course_rule(), mirrored exactly here and checked by scripts/check-life-config.mjs. answer: the index of the right option.

lessons.title: Greetings
points: As-salamu alaykum: peace be upon you, the greeting everyone uses.
The reply is wa alaykum as-salam: and upon you, peace.
Marhaba: hello. Ahlan wa sahlan: welcome.

lessons.title: Being polite
points: Shukran: thank you. Afwan: you're welcome.
Min fadlak (to a man) or min fadlik (to a woman): please.
Inshallah: God willing, said of anything in the future.

lessons.title: Gulf words you'll hear
points: Shlonak? (to a man) or shlonich? (to a woman): how are you?
Zain: good, fine. Yalla: let's go, come on.
Mashallah: said to admire something, a new car, a baby, a view.

lessons.title: Gahwa, Arabic coffee
points: Light, cardamom-spiced coffee poured into small cups called finjan, a little at a time.
It's offered and taken with the right hand, usually with dates.
When you've had enough, gently shake the cup from side to side as you hand it back.

lessons.title: In the majlis
points: The majlis is the sitting room where guests are received.
Take your shoes off at the door if your hosts do, and stand when an elder comes in.
Greet the most senior person first, and use your right hand to give and receive.

lessons.title: Respect in public
points: Dress modestly in mosques, government buildings and traditional places.
In Ramadan, don't eat, drink or smoke openly in public during fasting hours.
Ask before you photograph people, especially women and families.

options: Gently shake the cup as you hand it back

courses.title: Abu Dhabi: from pearls to a capital

lessons.title: A pearling town
points: For centuries Abu Dhabi lived from the sea: fishing and diving for natural pearls.
Qasr Al Hosn, a watchtower built in the 1760s and later a fort, is the city's oldest stone building.
Pearling collapsed in the 1930s when cheaper cultured pearls from Japan took the market.

lessons.title: Oil
points: Oil was found offshore at Umm Shaif in 1958.
Exports began in 1962 and paid for roads, schools, hospitals and homes.
Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan became ruler of Abu Dhabi in 1966.

lessons.title: The UAE
points: On 2 December 1971 the emirates joined to form the United Arab Emirates (Ras Al Khaimah joined in early 1972).
Sheikh Zayed was its first president, and Abu Dhabi its capital.
2 December is National Day, celebrated with flags, parades and fireworks.

quiz.q: Abu Dhabi's oldest stone building is…
Before oil, Abu Dhabi lived mainly from…

lessons.title: Hello and goodbye
points: Bonjour: hello (by day). Bonsoir: good evening.
Au revoir: goodbye. À bientôt: see you soon.
Always start with bonjour before you ask anything in a shop.

lessons.title: Please and thank you
points: S'il vous plaît: please. Merci: thank you. De rien: you're welcome.
Excusez-moi: excuse me. Pardon: sorry.
Je ne comprends pas: I don't understand.

lessons.title: At a café
points: Un café, s'il vous plaît: a coffee, please.
L'addition, s'il vous plaît: the bill, please.
Un, deux, trois: one, two, three.

quiz.q: To ask for the bill you say…

lessons.title: How solar panels work
points: Photovoltaic (PV) cells turn sunlight straight into electricity.
Energy is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh): a 1,000-watt heater running for an hour uses 1 kWh.
The Gulf's strong sun makes solar one of the cheapest ways to make power there.

lessons.title: The UAE's solar parks
points: Noor Abu Dhabi at Sweihan was one of the world's largest single solar plants when it opened in 2019.
Al Dhafra, south of the city, is bigger still, about 2 gigawatts.
Big plants are cleaned often: dust on the panels cuts their output.

lessons.title: Masdar City
points: Masdar City near the airport is built to use less energy and water.
Narrow shaded streets and a wind tower cool it, as in old Gulf towns.
Khalifa University's Masdar campus studies clean energy there.

quiz.q: Solar PV cells turn sunlight into…
Why are desert solar panels cleaned often?

lessons.title: Say exactly what you want
points: Vague prompts get vague answers: say the task, the audience and the length.
"Write a 3-line welcome for hotel guests in Abu Dhabi" beats "write a welcome".
Give the AI the facts it needs: names, dates, prices.

lessons.title: Show and shape
points: Give an example of what good looks like.
Ask for a format: a list, a table, short paragraphs.
Ask it to ask you questions if anything is missing.

lessons.title: Check it
points: AI can sound sure and still be wrong: check facts, numbers and names.
Never paste passwords or private details into a chatbot.
Edit the result: it's a first draft, not the final word.

options: Write a 3-line welcome for hotel guests in Abu Dhabi

quiz.q: You should never paste into a chatbot…

courses.title: Qatar's story: pearls, forts and independence

lessons.title: The pearling coast
points: Qatar's towns lived from pearl diving and fishing for centuries.
Al Zubarah in the north was a great pearling and trading town; it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013.
Cultured pearls in the 1930s ended the pearl trade.

lessons.title: Oil and gas
points: Oil was found at Dukhan on the west coast in 1939–1940.
The North Field, found offshore in 1971, is one of the world's largest natural gas fields.
Gas turned Qatar into one of the richest countries in the world.

lessons.title: A nation
points: Qatar became independent on 3 September 1971.
National Day is 18 December, marking the founding of the state in 1878.
Doha hosted the 2006 Asian Games and the 2022 FIFA World Cup.

quiz.q: Qatar's North Field holds huge amounts of…

lessons.title: Plan
points: Start with the goal: who it's for and what they should feel or learn.
Fix the budget, the date and the venue before anything else.
Book suppliers (sound, catering, staff) early and in writing.

lessons.title: Guests and safety
points: Plan how people arrive, queue, move and leave.
In Gulf heat: shade, water and first aid at every outdoor event.
Know the exits, the capacity and who is in charge if something goes wrong.

lessons.title: On the day, and after
points: A run-of-show lists every minute: who does what, and when.
Have a plan B for weather, no-shows and tech failures.
Afterwards: thank everyone, pay suppliers, ask guests what to improve.

quiz.q: The first thing to decide is…

options: A minute-by-minute plan of the day

quiz.q: At an outdoor summer event in Doha you must plan…

lessons.title: The session
points: Warm up for about 10 minutes: jogging, stretching, passing.
Small-sided games (4 v 4) give every player more touches of the ball.
Finish with a cool-down and a quick talk about what went well.

lessons.title: Coaching people
points: Praise effort, not just goals.
Keep instructions short: one idea at a time, then let them play.
Ask questions: "Where was the space?" teaches more than shouting.

lessons.title: Safety
points: Water breaks often, more in the heat; train in the evening in summer.
Check the pitch and the goals are safe and fixed down.
Stop at once for a head knock and get help.

lessons.title: Machboos
points: Qatar's best-loved dish: spiced rice cooked with chicken, lamb or fish.
Loomi, dried black lime, gives it its sour, smoky taste.
Baharat, a spice mix of cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and pepper, flavours the rice.

lessons.title: Harees and thareed
points: Harees: wheat and meat cooked for hours and beaten smooth, eaten in Ramadan and at Eid.
Thareed: thin bread soaked in a meat and vegetable stew.
Both are shared from one big dish.

lessons.title: Sweets and karak
points: Luqaimat: crisp fried dough balls drizzled with date syrup.
Karak: strong black tea boiled with milk, sugar and cardamom.
Dates and gahwa welcome every guest.

options: Tea boiled with milk and cardamom

lessons.title: Tools and direction
points: Arabic is written from right to left.
Calligraphers write with a qalam, a pen cut from reed or bamboo.
Letter sizes are measured in dots made by the pen's nib.

lessons.title: Kufic and Naskh
points: Kufic is angular and bold: the script of the earliest Qurans and of many building inscriptions.
Naskh is rounded and easy to read: used for books and most printing.
The Grand Mosque's qibla wall carries the 99 Names in Kufic.

lessons.title: Thuluth and Diwani
points: Thuluth is large and flowing, used for titles and on mosque walls.
Diwani, from the Ottoman court, curls and overlaps elegantly.
Look for them on Doha's buildings, coins and the Museum of Islamic Art's objects.

quiz.q: A calligrapher's reed pen is a…

lessons.title: Light
points: The golden hour, just after sunrise and before sunset, gives soft, warm light.
Midday sun is harsh: look for shade or shoot indoors.
West Bay's skyline glows at the blue hour, just after sunset.

lessons.title: Composition
points: Turn on the grid and put your subject on a third, not in the middle.
Use leading lines, like the Corniche or a road, to draw the eye in.
Get low or high for a fresh angle.

lessons.title: Simple habits
points: Wipe the lens: a smudge blurs everything.
Tap the screen to focus, and slide to adjust the brightness.
Ask before you photograph people.

quiz.q: The rule of thirds puts your subject…
options: On a third of the frame
